newsitem.title: USA: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.

text.p: Intel Corp., the leading maker of computer chips and a technology bellwether, stunned Wall Street Friday by warning its second-quarter results will be lower than expected due to weaker demand.

The unusually negative warning from a company that normally exceeds Wall Street's expectations triggered a massive sell-off in Intel and other technology stocks as investors feared the forecast was a sign of a general slowdown in personal computer sales.
However, by the end of the trading day, the stocks had recovered on views Intel's difficulties could be short-term.
After falling more than 15 percent to $140 a share, Intel closed off $12.27 at $151.50. More than 57 million shares traded, making Intel the most active stock on the New York Stock Exchange.

In a brief statement issued before the market opened, Intel said second-quarter profits would be below expectations and revenue would be about 5 percent to 10 percent below the first quarter's $6.4 billion. The company warned that gross margin, a key measure of profitability, could drop to around 60 percent from the first-quarter's 64 percent.

Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel, which supplies the chips used in more than 80 percent of the world's computers, blamed the shortfall on slower sales, particularly in Europe. Analysts said the warning raised concerns on Wall Street that worldwide demand for computers could be slowing.

"I'm in Taiwan at the moment and (PC assemblers) are saying that business is weak," said Drew Peck, analyst at investment bank Cowen & Co. "That would suggest Europe is not alone. The PC market has lulled a bit."
However, Compaq Computer Corp., which is among the first to get its hands on new Intel chips, said it has had a good quarter so far.

"Our order growth is well above that of the marketplace," Compaq Chief Financial Officer Earl Mason said. "We feel very good about the quarter and feel very bullish about the outlook for the rest of the year."

Some analysts said Intel's problems appear to be rooted in so-called second-tier PC makers in Europe and Asia that cannot get their hands on Intel's new Pentium II and Pentium MMX chips and are having a harder time selling computers.
However, most analysts said Intel should be able to overcome the supply problems as it boosts production levels.
Intel's bearish outlook comes as the company is facing renewed competition from rivals Cyrix Corp. and Advanced Micro Devices Inc., which could force Intel to cut prices on its Pentium chips.
On Friday, Cyrix Corp. introduced a new processor that will compete with the Intel Pentium II at half the price.
Cowen & Co.'s Peck said the competition has forced Intel to cut its prices, lowering its gross margins and profits.

In April, Intel said it expected revenue for the 1997 second quarter to be flat to slightly up from first-quarter revenue of $6.4 billion and gross margins to be flat to slightly down from 64 percent in the first quarter.
However, in light of the softer demand, Intel said revenues would now be lower than the first quarter and second-quarter gross margins were expected to be 60 percent "plus or minus a few points."

Over the long term, the company said, it expected its gross margin percentage "will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points," in line with previous company forecasts. Expenses are expected to rise 7 percent to 9 percent over the $1.3 billion it reported in the prior quarter.
In the second quarter of 1996, Intel reported a profit of $1.04 billion, or $1.17 a share, on revenues of $4.62 billion.
Prior to the company's outlook statement, analysts had expected Intel to report a second-quarter profit of $2.16 per share, according to the First Call service.
The sell-off quickly spread to other technology stocks. International Business Machines Corp. fell $1.375 to $86.50 on the New York Stock Exchange. Microsoft Corp. fell $1.875 to $124 on Nasdaq.
